Susceptible

/suh-SEP-tuh-bul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Susceptible means likely to be influenced, harmed, or affected by something specific; easily affected, usually followed by 'to.'

Because he skipped his flu shot, Marco was more susceptible to every cold that swept through the office that winter.

Worked Example

The car salesman quickly sensed that Mr. Okafor was susceptible to flattery. After a few well-placed compliments about his 'expert eye for quality,' the customer stopped comparing prices and agreed to pay nearly full sticker price for the sedan.

Mr. Okafor is easily influenced by compliments, which is exactly what it means to be susceptible to flattery.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

prone: likely to experience something, often something bad

impressionable: easily influenced by others

sensitive: quick to be affected by outside conditions

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

immune: protected from an effect or disease

resistant: able to withstand something's effects

Where it sits · how easily outside forces get through — open → susceptible → defenseless

open vs. susceptible: A person who is open to suggestions simply listens willingly, while a susceptible person is easily swayed whether they mean to be or not.

defenseless vs. susceptible: Being susceptible means you can be affected more easily than most, but being defenseless means you have no protection left at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — sus-

Prefix — sus-: a form of sub-, up from under

Root — cept

Root — cept: from Latin capere, to take

Suffix — -ible

Suffix — -ible: able to be

Put it together

Put it together: Susceptible stacks sus-, a form of the Latin prefix sub- meaning 'up from under,' onto the root capere, 'to take,' plus the suffix -ible, 'able to be.' Something susceptible can literally be 'taken up' by an outside influence, whether that influence is a cold virus, a catchy slogan, or a flatterer's compliment.

Use the root in a new word: intercept

Use the root in a new word: intercept: The goalkeeper raced out to intercept the pass, literally 'taking' the ball between two players, from the same Latin root capere that hides inside susceptible.

Word Choice

neutral

Susceptible is almost always followed by 'to': susceptible to colds, susceptible to flattery, susceptible to peer pressure. Do not confuse it with vulnerable; vulnerable implies a more serious exposure to real harm or danger, while susceptible often describes milder, everyday influence.
